newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Smurfit sees 1997 as difficult year.
newsitem.headline: Smurfit sees 1997 as difficult year.

text.p: Irish paper and packaging manufacturer Jefferson Smurfit Group Plc said on Tuesday that 1997 will be a very difficult year for the industry but believed prices may have bottomed out.
"Price weakness continues in most paper grades," Smurfit said in a results statement which showed a drop in pre-tax profit to 204 million punts for the group from 420 million the previous year.

"I believe prices have bottomed out and that the industry may be close to its turning point," chairman Michael Smurfit said. "A resumption of seasonal strength in the latter half of 1997 may support the beginnings of a sustained industry upturn."
Smurfit said that while it could no longer 'buck the trend' to the extent that it did when the group had a smaller market share, it would continue to emphasise profitability over production.

"It is clear to us that biggest is not always best," Smurfit said. "We try where possible, to buy rather than build paper making capacity. We limit capacity expansion and base capital expenditure decisions on real not anticipated demand," it said.
Smurfit, which showed a 52 percent drop in pre-tax profits in 1996, said the earnings decline had been mainly caused by excess U.S. containerboard capacity.
It said between 1994 and 1997, the U.S. industry will have added 5.9 million tons of additional capacity; an annualised capacity growth rate of 4.5 percent.
Growth in capacity broadly represents twice that required by 'normal' demand growth, it said.
Smurfit said it believed the industry's ability to return shareholder value would be driven by further consolidation and greater discipline.
"Clearly, the market will not accept for long an industry which, as a recent survey has shown, did not earn its cost of capital in seven of the last 10 years," it said.
Smurfit said disciplined use of capital was key, both in the good times and the bad.
"Indiscriminate application of capital in the good times will only serve to presage the industry's next cyclical trough," Smurfit said.
